THINGS HIDDEN 21: Jean-Michel Oughourlian Interview

THINGS HIDDEN 21: Jean-Michel Oughourlian Interview

Sep 29, 2020
In this Things Hidden conversation, David Gornoski and Shannon Braswell are joined by Jean-Michel Oughourlian, psychologist and author of 'The Mimetic Brain.' Oughourlian starts the discussion with an insider's perspective as Girard's collaborator and how he found breakthroughs in the field of psychotherapy upon studying mimetic theory.
"The mirror neuron is something fantastic," Oughourlian remarks, "because if you experiment, if you put a CT scan or PET scan on your own head and mine, and I'm drinking a glass of water, and you are on the other side of the Atlantic just looking at me, in both our brains the same regions will be activated the same way. In other words, whether I do the action or whether you look at it, the brain functions the same way--it mirrors what I'm doing."
How does this discovery relate to the right and left-hemisphere brain study by Iain McGilchrist? How has mimetic theory helped Jean-Michel Oughourlian in the field of psychotheraphy?
"What I try to do when I see a patient is not so much find out what he is suffering from but to find out who he is suffering from. In _[Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World](https://www.sup.org/books/religious-studies/things-hidden-foundation-world)_ , you referred to your project as "interdividual psychology" (1978),

...

MŁ: Where does the power of models come from in our lives?

JMO: Mimeticism in the social world is like gravity in the physical world. The model is always a fixed point of reference.

...

We can choose our relationship to the model, but we cannot bypass the models themselves.

MŁ: Why?

JMO: Because of the structure of our brain. We have no choice because everyone's brain has mirror neurons. This was a big discovery in neuroscience, which showed that mimeticism has a biological basis.

...

Today's innovative corporations are based on a mimetic mechanism, the release of mimetic desire on a global scale.

...

MŁ: This is reminiscent of the story of the young schizophrenic you cite in _[Mimetic Brain](https://msupress.org/9781611861891/the-mimetic-brain/)_ (2016). His model was an uncle who ran a huge company with great success. The boy wanted to follow in his footsteps and be employed by him, but his uncle did not agree, which led to a mental crisis. According to Bateson's model of schizophrenia, which you refer to, the model implies a double bind for the imitator. On the one hand, it says: be like me; and on the other: I will not let you be like me. These conflicting desires of our model lead to the breakdown of our personality.

Biographie de Jean-Michel Oughourlian

Neuropsychiatre (il a dirigé le service de psychiatrie de l'Hôpital américain de Neuilly), psychologue (ayant enseigné en Sorbonne) et disciple de René Girard, avec qui il a co-écrit le best-seller Des choses cachées depuis la fondation du monde , Jean-Michel Oughourlian a mis en place la psychologie mimétique et exerce, depuis cinquante ans, à travers son prisme. Il est l'auteur de plusieurs ouvrages, dont Notre troisième cerveau (2013) et Cet autre qui m'obsède (2017), publiés chez Albin Michel. Les Mécanismes du désir a paru chez Robert Laffont en 2024.
